content: 1. High-certainty evidence supports the use of interventions that involve the process and discussion of implementation strategies, as well as task-sharing approaches, to improve linkage to HIV care and antiretroviral therapy (ART) initiation. 2. Moderate-certainty evidence highlights the importance of family and peer support in facilitating linkage to care. 3. HIV programs must address barriers to care and ART initiation, particularly for populations facing multiple structural and individual challenges in accessing services. 4. Effective interventions, such as peer support, have demonstrated benefits across various stages of the HIV care cascade and are being implemented in diverse settings. 5. For pregnant and breastfeeding women, integrating HIV services with maternal, newborn, and child health services can reduce disengagement from care. If integration is not feasible, peer support systems can help ensure linkage between antenatal care and ART services. 6. Retesting during pregnancy and postpartum is critical, especially in high HIV burden settings. Pregnant women with unknown or negative HIV status should be retested in the third trimester, and postpartum retesting may be considered in high-incidence regions or for women with partners living with unsuppressed HIV. 7. For children, poor retention in care, particularly among infants diagnosed through early infant diagnosis programs, can be addressed by using point-of-care testing, SMS or GPRS printers to expedite results, and family-centered care models. 8. Adolescents may struggle with coping after an HIV diagnosis due to developmental changes, limited health awareness, and challenges navigating health services. Adolescent-friendly linkage services, peer-based interventions, community-based services, and mobile technology can improve linkage and retention. 9. Key populations, such as men who have sex with men, sex workers, transgender individuals, people in prisons, and people who inject drugs, face unique barriers to accessing HIV services due to stigma, discrimination, and criminalization. Community-based service delivery, including peer-led models, has proven effective in these settings. 10. Continuity of care for people transitioning between prisons and the community is essential. Providing several months of ART and addressing housing, health insurance, and provider access can mitigate treatment interruptions. 11. Differentiated service delivery (DSD) for HIV treatment is a person-centered approach that adapts services to meet the diverse needs of people living with HIV while optimizing health system resources. 12. DSD models should address the needs of specific populations, such as children, adolescents, pregnant and breastfeeding women, and key populations, and can be adapted for low-prevalence or emergency settings. 13. ART adherence clubs, a group model managed by healthcare workers, have shown high retention and viral suppression rates, with significant benefits for populations such as adolescents, postnatal women, and those with prior adherence challenges. 14. Client-managed group models, such as community adherence groups, have demonstrated improved retention and reduced costs for clients, while also decongesting clinics and reducing healthcare worker workloads. 15. Multi-month ART refills and dispensing can be integrated into DSD models, benefiting both health systems and clients, including children older than two years. 16. National guidelines should include clear linkage strategies, policies, and monitoring mechanisms to support rapid ART initiation and effective service delivery. 17. Research is needed to evaluate strategies for improving linkage to care, disaggregating effects by gender, age, and key populations, and assessing the cost-effectiveness of interventions. 18. Further studies should explore the role of digital media platforms in facilitating linkage and rapid ART initiation, as well as strategies to re-engage people living with HIV who have declined ART or been lost to follow-up. 19. Differentiated service delivery models for HIV treatment should be designed to address clinical needs and contextual factors, ensuring equitable access to care for all populations. 20. ART provision should not depend on receiving other services, and clinical consultations should be separated from ART refill visits when appropriate. 21. Psychosocial support can be aligned with clinical consultations and ART refills or provided separately through community and peer support systems. 22. Group models managed by healthcare workers or clients, as well as individual facility-based or community-based models, offer flexibility and additional benefits for HIV treatment delivery. 23. Evidence supports the effectiveness and acceptability of adherence clubs and community-led ART delivery models in improving retention, viral suppression, and client satisfaction. 24. Differentiated service delivery models should be tailored to meet the needs of diverse populations, including those with advanced HIV disease, high viral loads, or comorbidities, to ensure optimal outcomes.
